title: Are Higher Rates Cause to Add More Fixed Income? | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional argues that the post-GFC-high bond yields of recent years are not a reason to shift weight from equities into fixed income, because stock discount rates already embed the level of interest rates. Using 1927-2025 data, the average US equity premium was 9.9% in years starting with a below-median one-month T-bill rate versus 8.1% in above-median years, a gap that fails a t-test for statistical reliability.

insights.claim: In years starting with a one-month US Treasury bill rate below its historical median, the average annual US equity premium was about 9.9%, versus 8.1% in above-median rate years, over 1927-2025.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The raw spread between low- and high-rate regimes is only ~1.8 percentage points, far too small to justify a strategic tilt out of stocks when cash yields rise.

insights.claim: Because the discount rates used to value stocks already incorporate prevailing interest rates, higher bond yields should mechanically raise expected stock returns as well, leaving the stock-over-bond premium unchanged.
insights.speaker: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
insights.so_what: The common 'bonds finally yield something, so de-risk' argument double-counts rates; the correct comparison is the spread, not the absolute bond yield.
insights.quote: All else equal, higher bond yields should lead to higher expected stock returns. In other words, the premium for stocks over bonds may not shrink just because of higher rates.
